title: 2026 State of the Corporate Law Department Report: GCs Align Strategy to Corporate Imperatives, but C-Suites Want More
pub: Thomson Reuters Institute (open summary article of the registration-gated report)
author: Thomson Reuters Institute

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The report accepts that AI is producing early operational gains while tool adoption alone does not establish successful transformation. It materially extends the cluster from workflow performance into buyer-side governance by arguing that legal departments should measure whether AI-created capacity advances business objectives and commercial outcomes.
qs: Although almost half of all corporate legal departments have some type of enterprise-wide GenAI tool, according to the survey, very few are collecting success metrics around AI’s implementation or linking its use to business revenue.
Put a different way, many legal departments are focused on *unlocking *capacity, rather than *deploying* capacity in a business-centric way — much to the chagrin of their C-Suites.

st.t: Buyer transformation: Legal departments may capture AI gains
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s proposition that legal departments may capture AI gains only if they can absorb technology operationally and convert efficiency into measurable business outcomes. It reports growing AI availability and early efficiency benefits, but weak implementation metrics and limited linkage to revenue; its emphasis on deploying freed capacity strategically reinforces the identified organisational bottleneck. Expected increases in outside-counsel spending temper claims of immediate insourcing but do not undermine the core position.

kp.k: GCs and executives sharply disagree on legal's contribution
kp.d: The Thomson Reuters Institute's open summary reports that 86% of surveyed GCs see legal as a significant business contributor, compared with 17% of other C-Suite executives; 42% of those executives say legal contributes little or nothing. The article interprets this as a gap between legal departments' operational progress and executive recognition, recommending that GCs prove rather than merely assert business alignment. The supplied summary does not specify sample sizes or survey methodology; the full report is not held.
qs: 86% of GCs surveyed said they viewed the legal function as a significant contributor.
However, only 17% of other C-Suite executives said the same — and 42% said legal contributes little or not at all.

kp.k: Resource constraints coexist with expected outside counsel spending increases
kp.d: Nearly half of GCs identify staffing and resource constraints as their top barrier to delivering additional value. As of the fourth quarter of 2025, 36% expect overall outside counsel spending to increase over the following year, versus 20% planning decreases. These are spending expectations, not observed changes; the summary also reports expectations of continued high spending in regulatory work and mergers and acquisitions.
qs: Nearly half of GCs cited staffing and resource constraints as the top barrier they face to delivering additional value.

As of the fourth quarter of 2025, more than one-third (36%) of GCs said they expect to increase overall spend on outside counsel over the next year, while only 20% said they plan to decrease their spend.

kp.k: Technology and AI gain strategic priority
kp.d: The summary presents technology as a principal response to resource and cost pressures. Its takeaways say the proportion of GCs calling AI a strategic imperative doubled, while the body describes a doubling in those mentioning technology as a strategic priority entering 2026 relative to the prior year. Neither statement supplies the underlying percentages. The report also describes emerging AI benefits in efficiency and time available for strategic work without quantifying them.
qs: the proportion of GCs calling AI a *strategic imperative* has doubled.
the proportion of GCs mentioning technology as a strategic priority entering 2026 doubled over the year prior.
Legal departments have begun to feel positive effects of AI in their own organizations

kp.k: GenAI availability outpaces measurement of business outcomes
kp.d: According to the survey as summarized, almost half of corporate legal departments have some type of enterprise-wide GenAI tool, but very few collect AI implementation success metrics or link use to business revenue. The article distinguishes freeing capacity through technology from deploying that capacity toward business objectives, arguing that the latter is what executives want. It provides no precise percentage for departments measuring success.
qs: Although almost half of all corporate legal departments have some type of enterprise-wide GenAI tool, according to the survey, very few are collecting success metrics around AI’s implementation or linking its use to business revenue.
many legal departments are focused on *unlocking *capacity, rather than *deploying* capacity in a business-centric way

kp.k: Legal operations increasingly use data and broader performance metrics
kp.d: The article describes changes over the past several years: greater technology use, particularly AI, adjusted hiring practices, and broader metrics for evaluating outside counsel and internal operations. These are qualitative descriptions of in-house operational change; the summary does not identify specific hiring changes or quantify workforce effects.
qs: GCs have adjusted their hiring practices to conform with the modern corporation, taking new ways of working into account.
And they have embraced data-driven decision-making, evaluating outside counsel and their own operations alike with a wider suite of new metrics and KPIs.

kp.k: Legal advice should enable decisions and demonstrate business value
kp.d: The report recommends translating operational efficiency into business outcomes by linking advice to business objectives, contextualizing legal spending as a percentage of revenue, and managing risk to support business imperatives. A quoted retail GC describes their company's demand for decision guidance rather than legal opinions alone. The article extends this business-oriented approach to AI and technology and calls for active communication of legal's contribution.
qs: This can take a number of different forms, such as explicitly tying advice to client business objectives, presenting legal spend in the context of the business by showing it as a percentage of revenue, or approaching risk management with the goal of aiding business imperatives.
“When we have a risky legal subject, the company never prefers just to see the legal opinion,” said one retail GC. “They’re also requesting you to drive them how to make a decision.”
AI and technology should also be approached in this same way, the report argues.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Thomson Reuters Institute reports that AI is improving corporate legal departments’ efficiency and freeing time for strategic work, but departments have not generally demonstrated how that capacity contributes to business outcomes.
pts.d: The summary attributes emerging operational benefits to AI and presents technology as a response to resource and cost pressures. It reports accelerating adoption and strategic importance: almost half of corporate legal departments have some type of enterprise-wide GenAI tool. Its key takeaways say the proportion of GCs calling AI a strategic imperative doubled, whereas the body describes a doubling in technology being mentioned as a strategic priority; these formulations should not be treated as an identical, precisely specified AI adoption measure. The Institute argues that unlocking capacity is insufficient without deploying it toward business objectives and measuring results. This is an account of current changes and a recommendation about their use, not a quantified forecast of future productivity, revenue, or job displacement.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered consists of survey findings and qualitative statements attributed to the Institute’s 2026 report; the held summary provides no quantified measurement of AI’s operational or business impact.
pts.d: The adoption and priority claims are presented as report or survey findings. The summary gives neither exact adoption percentages beyond 'almost half' nor baseline percentages for the reported doubling, and does not specify how many departments collect AI success metrics. Efficiency and time-saving benefits are described qualitatively, without measured hours saved, cost reductions, revenue effects, or causal tests. The wider survey findings—86% of GCs versus 17% of other C-Suite executives seeing legal as a significant contributor, and nearly half of GCs identifying resource constraints—provide context, not evidence that AI caused the perception gap or solved the constraints. Only the open summary is held; sample sizes, methodology, and underlying report detail are not provided in it.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The claims concern changes over recent years and conditions entering 2026; converting AI-enabled efficiency into business value is framed as the next step, without a deadline.
pts.d: The summary locates increased technology use over the past several years, the doubling in technology’s strategic priority entering 2026 relative to the prior year, and emerging AI benefits in the present. It does not explicitly date every AI survey measure. The fourth-quarter 2025 date applies specifically to outside-counsel spending expectations, not expressly to all AI findings. Business impact is framed as requiring purposeful use of freed capacity, alignment with business objectives, success measurement, and communication of legal’s contribution. The article does not predict when these changes will produce demonstrable results.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The affected actors are corporate legal departments and GCs, with C-Suite leaders and the wider business positioned as the intended beneficiaries of AI-enabled capacity.
pts.d: The claims concern the buyer side of legal services: in-house departments using AI to improve efficiency and manage resource and cost pressures. GCs face expectations to redirect operational gains toward strategic business work and demonstrate their value to corporate leadership. C-Suite executives seek contributions to business success rather than operational improvement alone. The source does not identify AI-driven displacement of particular legal roles, changes in law-firm staffing or pricing, or effects on public access to justice. Its outside-counsel spending expectations are not expressly attributed to AI.
